tips.title: One fraction does both jobs
tips.body: A sector is $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of a whole circle. Multiply that **same fraction** by the **circumference** for the arc, or by the **area** for the sector area. There is only one idea here, used twice.

tips.title: Perimeter is not the arc
tips.body: The **perimeter** of a sector is the curved arc **plus the two straight radii**. Giving only the arc is the most frequently lost mark in the topic, because the arc looks like the whole edge until you notice the two cut sides.

tips.title: Does the fraction look right?
tips.body: A **90°** sector is a **quarter**, **180°** is a **half**, **120°** is a **third**. Work out what fraction of the circle you expect, and check the answer is roughly that share of the full circumference or area.

tips.title: Leave it in terms of π
tips.body: If the question says "in terms of $\pi$", **do not press the π key**. A 45° sector of radius 8 has area $\frac{1}{8} \times 64\pi = 8\pi$ — exact, quicker, and impossible to round wrongly.

tips.title: Radius, not diameter
tips.body: The formulas use the **radius**. If a question gives a **diameter**, halve it first. Using the diameter makes an arc twice as long and an area **four times** too big.

steps.title: A sector is a fraction of a circle
steps.body:
**A sector is a slice of a circle** — the region between two radii and the arc joining them. The angle at the centre, $\theta$, decides how big a slice it is.

**The whole circle is 360°, so the slice is $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of it.** That single fraction is the entire topic. Everything else follows:

$$\text{arc length} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$$
$$\text{sector area} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$$

The **first** is that fraction of the **circumference**. The **second** is the same fraction of the **area**. There is nothing new to memorise beyond the two circle formulas you already have.

**The familiar cases are a good check.** A 90° sector is $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$ of the circle — a quarter. A 180° sector is a **semicircle**, exactly half. A 120° sector is a third. If your answer is not roughly that share of the whole circle, something has gone wrong.

**Two words that are easy to confuse.** The **arc** is only the curved edge. The **perimeter** of the sector is the arc **plus the two radii**, because the slice has two straight cut sides as well.

steps.title: Exact answers, and working backwards
steps.body:
**"In terms of $\pi$" means leave $\pi$ in the answer.** A 45° sector of radius 8 has area $8\pi$ cm². That **is** the answer — writing 25.13 instead loses the mark, because it is a rounded approximation of an exact quantity the question asked for exactly.

Exact form is also **easier**. The fractions cancel: $\frac{1}{8} \times 64\pi = 8\pi$ needs no calculator at all, and nothing can be mis-rounded.

**Working backwards.** Questions often give the arc or the area and ask for the **angle** or the **radius**. The method does not change — put the numbers into the same formula and solve.

For example, a sector of radius 6 has an arc of $4\pi$. What is the angle?

$$\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6 = 4\pi$$
$$\frac{\theta}{360} \times 12\pi = 4\pi$$

The $\pi$ cancels from both sides, leaving $\frac{\theta}{360} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$, so $\theta = 120°$.

**Notice that $\pi$ cancelled.** In a backwards question it almost always does, so keeping the answer in terms of $\pi$ makes the algebra shorter as well as exact.

**Check the angle is under 360°.** An angle above 360° means the arc given was longer than the whole circumference, which cannot happen.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Write the fraction down before anything else.** $\frac{\theta}{360}$ is the whole topic, and it is identical for the arc and for the area. Having it on the page also gives you a free check: a 90° sector must be a **quarter** of the circle, a 120° sector a **third**.

**Perimeter means all the way round.** The perimeter of a sector is the **arc plus both radii**, and leaving off the two straight sides is the single most common lost mark here. The word *perimeter* — not *arc* — is the signal, so read it deliberately.

**Halve a diameter before using it.** For an **arc**, using the diameter makes the answer **twice** too big. For an **area**, it makes it **four times** too big, because the radius is squared. A wrong answer exactly four times the right one is the signature of this error.

**Leave $\pi$ in when exact form is asked for.** $8\pi$ is the answer, not 25.13. Exact form is also less work: the fractions cancel and there is nothing to round. When a question does want a decimal, carry the full value and round **once**, at the end — rounding $\pi$ to 3.14 partway through will not survive a 2-decimal-place mark scheme.

**Backwards questions use the same formula.** Given an arc or an area, substitute and solve for the angle or the radius. The $\pi$ almost always **cancels from both sides**, which is another reason to keep exact form as long as possible. Then check the result is possible: an angle must be **under 360°**, and a radius must be positive.

**Watch for compound shapes.** A shape made of a sector and a triangle needs the two parts worked out **separately** and then combined — and when it is a perimeter rather than an area, some edges are **internal** and must not be counted. Sketching the outline and tracing round it with a finger is the reliable way to see which edges are on the outside.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- A **sector** is a slice of a circle between two radii and an arc.
- It is $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of the whole circle — **one fraction, used twice**.
- **Arc length** $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$, that fraction of the **circumference**.
- **Sector area** $= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$, the same fraction of the **area**.
- **90° is a quarter**, **120° a third**, **180° a semicircle** — useful checks.
- **Perimeter** of a sector $=$ **arc $+ 2r$**, because of the two straight sides.
- Giving the arc when the perimeter was asked for is the commonest lost mark.
- The formulas use the **radius**: halve a **diameter** before using it.
- A diameter used as a radius makes an **area four times** too big.
- **"In terms of $\pi$"** means leave $\pi$ in: $8\pi$, not 25.13.
- Exact form is also quicker, because the fractions cancel.
- **Backwards questions** use the same formula: substitute and solve.
- In a backwards question the **$\pi$ usually cancels** from both sides.
- Check the angle comes out **under 360°**.
- For **compound shapes**, work out each part separately and ignore internal edges in a perimeter.

questions.prompt: What fraction of a circle is a 120° sector?
questions.solution: $\frac{120}{360} = \frac{1}{3}$, so it is a **third** of the circle — a third of its circumference and a third of its area.

questions.prompt: Which formula gives the arc length of a sector?
questions.solution: The arc is that fraction of the **circumference**, so $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$. The second option is the sector **area**.

questions.prompt: Find the arc length of a sector of radius 10 cm with angle 72°, in cm to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution: $\frac{72}{360} = \frac{1}{5}$ and the circumference is $20\pi$, so the arc is $4\pi = 12.57$ cm.

questions.prompt: A sector has a radius of 5 cm. What is the perimeter made of?
questions.solution: The perimeter is the arc **plus both radii**: $\text{arc} + 5 + 5 = \text{arc} + 10$ cm. A sector has two straight cut sides.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a sector of radius 10 cm with angle 72°, in cm² to 2 decimal places.
Find the area of a sector of radius 6 cm with angle 120°, in cm² to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution: $\frac{120}{360} = \frac{1}{3}$ and the circle has area $36\pi$, so the sector is $12\pi = 37.7$ cm².

questions.prompt: Find the perimeter of a sector of radius 8 cm with angle 45°, in cm to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution: The arc is $\frac{1}{8} \times 16\pi = 2\pi = 6.28$ cm. The perimeter adds **both radii**: $6.28 + 8 + 8 = 22.28$ cm. Giving only the arc is the commonest error here.

questions.prompt: A question gives the diameter of a sector rather than the radius. What must you do first?
questions.solution: **Halve it.** The formulas use the **radius**. Using a diameter makes an arc twice too long and an area **four times** too big, because the radius is squared.

questions.prompt: A 90° sector of a circle of radius 4 cm has what area, in terms of $\pi$?
questions.solution: $\frac{90}{360} = \frac{1}{4}$, and the circle has area $\pi \times 4^2 = 16\pi$. A quarter of that is $4\pi$ cm².

questions.prompt: A question asks for a sector area "in terms of $\pi$" and you calculate $8\pi$. What should you write?
questions.solution: Leave it as **$8\pi$**. That is the exact value asked for; 25.13 is a rounded approximation and loses the mark, while 8 has dropped the $\pi$.

questions.prompt: A sector of radius 6 cm has an arc length of $4\pi$ cm. Find the angle at the centre, in degrees.
questions.solution: Substitute into the same formula: $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 12\pi = 4\pi$. The $\pi$ **cancels from both sides**, leaving $\frac{\theta}{360} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$, so $\theta = 120°$. Check: 120° is under 360°, as it must be.

questions.prompt: A student uses a diameter of 12 cm as the radius when finding a sector area. How wrong is the answer?
questions.solution: The radius is **squared** in the area formula, so doubling it multiplies the area by $2^2 = 4$. The answer is **four times** too big. For an **arc**, where the radius is not squared, the same mistake would only double it.
options: A quarter of the correct value

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to keep $\pi$ in the working when a question asks for the angle of a sector?
questions.solution: In a backwards question, $\pi$ appears on **both sides** of the equation — in the arc you were given and in the circumference — so it **cancels**. Keeping it symbolic avoids a calculator step and avoids rounding an exact quantity.

markScheme.description: the π cancels from both sides

options: The π cancels from both sides, making the algebra shorter
Angles must always be given in terms of π
The calculator cannot divide by π accurately
It converts the answer into radians automatically

questions.prompt: A student gives the perimeter of a sector of radius 7 cm as equal to its arc length. What have they forgotten?
questions.solution: A sector is bounded by the **arc and two radii**. The perimeter is $\text{arc} + 7 + 7 = \text{arc} + 14$ cm. The word *perimeter* means all the way round, and the two cut edges are part of that boundary.
options: The two straight radii, worth 14 cm
To convert the angle into a fraction

questions.prompt: A semicircle has radius 8 cm. Find its perimeter, in cm to 2 decimal places.
questions.solution: A semicircle is a 180° sector, so its arc is half the circumference: $\frac{1}{2} \times 16\pi = 8\pi = 25.13$ cm. The perimeter adds the **diameter**, which is the two radii together: $25.13 + 16 = 41.13$ cm. The straight edge is easy to forget because it looks like a base rather than part of the boundary.

questions.prompt: When finding the perimeter of a shape made from a sector joined to a triangle, which edges are counted?
questions.solution: A perimeter is the distance around the **outside**. Where the two parts join, that edge is **internal** and is not part of the boundary. Tracing round the outline is the reliable way to see which edges count — adding every edge of both parts double-counts the join.
options: Only the edges on the outside of the whole shape
Every edge of both the sector and the triangle
The arc and all three sides of the triangle

questions.prompt: Explain how the arc length and area of a sector are found, why the same fraction appears in both, and how the perimeter of a sector differs from its arc length.
questions.solution:
A **sector** is the slice of a circle between two radii and the arc joining them, and the angle $\theta$ at the centre decides how large a slice it is.

Since a full turn is **360°**, the sector is $\frac{\theta}{360}$ of the whole circle. That single fraction is the whole idea, and everything else follows from it.

The **arc length** is that fraction of the **circumference**:

$$\text{arc} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$$

The **sector area** is the **same** fraction of the **area**:

$$\text{area} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$$

The fraction is identical in both because slicing the circle at a given angle takes the same proportion of everything about it. A 90° cut takes a quarter of the way round the edge and a quarter of the space inside. So there is really only one formula here, applied to the circumference in one case and to the area in the other — nothing new to memorise beyond the two circle formulas.

For a sector of radius 8 cm with an angle of 45°, the fraction is $\frac{45}{360} = \frac{1}{8}$. The circumference is $16\pi$, so the arc is $\frac{1}{8} \times 16\pi = 2\pi \approx 6.28$ cm. The area of the circle is $64\pi$, so the sector area is $\frac{1}{8} \times 64\pi = 8\pi \approx 25.13$ cm².

The **perimeter** is different from the arc, and this is where most marks are lost. The **arc** is only the **curved** edge. But a sector is a slice, and a slice has **two straight cut sides** as well — the two radii. So the perimeter, which means the distance all the way round the boundary, is

$$\text{perimeter} = \text{arc} + 2r$$

For the sector above, that is $6.28 + 8 + 8 = 22.28$ cm, not 6.28 cm. Reading the word *perimeter* rather than *arc* is the whole of it.

A good **check** on any answer is the fraction itself. A **90°** sector must be a **quarter** of the circle, **120°** a **third**, and **180°** a **semicircle**. If the answer is not roughly that share of the whole circumference or area, something has gone wrong. It is also worth confirming that a **radius**, not a diameter, was used — a diameter mistaken for a radius makes an area **four times** too big, since the radius is squared.

questions.prompt: A sector of a circle has radius 6 cm and an arc length of $4\pi$ cm. Find the angle at the centre and the area of the sector, giving the area in terms of $\pi$, and explain how you check each answer.
questions.solution:
Running a sector question **backwards** needs no new formula. I put what I know into the ordinary arc formula and solve for the part that is missing.

$$\text{arc} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$$

With $r = 6$ and an arc of $4\pi$:

$$\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi \times 6 = 4\pi$$
$$\frac{\theta}{360} \times 12\pi = 4\pi$$

The $\pi$ appears on **both sides**, so it **cancels**:

$$\frac{\theta}{360} = \frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$$

This is worth pausing on: the fraction $\frac{1}{3}$ is exactly what the sector is — a **third** of the circle. So

$$\theta = \frac{1}{3} \times 360 = 120°$$

Keeping the arc as $4\pi$ rather than converting it to 12.57 is what made this short. Had I worked in decimals I would have needed a calculator and risked a rounding error, and the neat $\frac{1}{3}$ would have been hidden inside an untidy decimal.

**For the area**, I use the same fraction:

$$\text{area} = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 = \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 6^2 = \frac{1}{3} \times 36\pi = 12\pi \text{ cm}^2$$

Since the question asks for the area **in terms of $\pi$**, the answer is **$12\pi$ cm²**. Writing 37.7 cm² instead would replace an exact value with a rounded one and lose the mark.

**Checking the angle.** It must be **less than 360°**, since a sector cannot be more than a whole circle — and 120° is. It should also be consistent with the arc I was given: an arc of $4\pi$ against a full circumference of $12\pi$ is exactly a third of the way round, and a third of 360° is 120°. The two agree.

**Checking the area.** The whole circle has area $36\pi$, and a third of that is $12\pi$, which is what I found. As a rough numerical check, $36\pi \approx 113$ cm² and a third of that is about 38 cm², matching $12\pi \approx 37.7$ cm².

Both answers therefore describe the same sector: a third of a circle of radius 6 cm.

examTechnique.body:
Write $\frac{\theta}{360}$ down first — it is the same fraction for the arc and for the area, and it gives you an instant check on the size of the answer.

Read **arc** or **perimeter** carefully: a perimeter adds the **two radii**. Halve any **diameter** before using it, and leave $\pi$ in when exact form is asked for.
examinerErrors: Giving the arc length when the **perimeter** was asked for.
Using a **diameter** as the radius, making an area four times too big.
Writing a decimal when the question said **in terms of $\pi$**.
Using the area formula for the arc, or the other way round.
Rounding $\pi$ to 3.14 partway through the working.
Forgetting the straight diameter in the perimeter of a semicircle.
Counting internal edges in the perimeter of a compound shape.
Giving an area in cm rather than cm².
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the **fraction $\frac{\theta}{360}$ first** and uses it to sanity-check the result — a 90° sector really is a quarter of the circle. It reads **arc** against **perimeter** deliberately and adds the **two radii** when the perimeter is wanted. It keeps answers **in terms of $\pi$** when asked, and notices that in a backwards question the $\pi$ **cancels**, so exact form is quicker as well as more accurate. It halves a **diameter** without prompting, and for a compound shape traces the **outside** edges rather than adding up every side.
